item.title: Cisco IOS and IOS-XE Upgrade Guide: Catalyst Switches and ISR Routers
item.description: Step-by-step Cisco IOS and IOS-XE software upgrade for Catalyst switches (2960, 3560, 3850, 9200, 9300, 9500) and routers (ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8000) — flash checks, ROMMON, install mode, bundle mode, MD5 and rollback.
item.content:encoded:
Most Cisco upgrades fail before the first command is typed: the wrong image for the platform, too little space in flash, a ROMMON that is too old for the target release, or a boot variable that points nowhere. This guide puts the checks first and the commands second.

It covers both families you meet in practice:

Family Typical models Software File system Upgrade method
Classic Catalyst switches 2960, 2960-X, 3560, 3750 IOS flash: archive download-sw or .bin + boot system
IOS-XE Catalyst switches 3650, 3850, 9200, 9300, 9400, 9500 IOS-XE flash: (on some models bootflash:) Install mode (packages.conf)
IOS-XE routers ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8200/8300, Catalyst 8000V IOS-XE bootflash: Install mode or bundle mode
Classic IOS routers ISR G2, C900 IOS flash: .bin + boot system

The commands are the ones I use in the field on Catalyst switches and ISR routers. IP addresses and paths in the examples are placeholders.

1. Check the Platform Before Anything Else

File System: flash: or bootflash:?

Do not assume. Ask the device:

show file systems
dir

Classic Catalyst switches and Catalyst 9200/9300 use flash:. ISR and Catalyst 8000 routers use bootflash:. On many IOS-XE platforms one name is an alias for the other. Use whatever the device shows. Every command in this guide works with either name.

Model, Version and Boot Mode

show version
show inventory
show boot            ! switches
show bootvar         ! routers
show install summary ! IOS-XE only

Write down:

  • Exact model and platform family. An image for an ISR 4300 does not boot on an ISR 4400. The platform family is in the file name, for example isr4300-universalk9, c1100-universalk9, cat9k_iosxe.
  • Current version.
  • Boot mode on IOS-XE. If the boot variable points to packages.conf, the device runs in install mode. If it points to a .bin file, it runs in bundle mode.

Free Space

dir shows the free bytes at the bottom. An IOS-XE image is large, and install mode needs extra space to extract the packages. If space is tight, clean up first:

install remove inactive   ! IOS-XE install mode: removes unused packages
delete flash:<old-image>.bin

2. Read the Release Notes: Upgrade Path and ROMMON

Two things in the release notes decide whether the upgrade works:

  • Upgrade path. Some jumps are not supported directly. Cisco documents, for example, that Catalyst 9500 switches in bundle mode should go from 16.x to 17.x through an intermediate release, while install mode supports the direct jump.
  • Minimum ROMMON version. Every IOS-XE release needs a minimum ROMMON (boot loader) version. If the device has an older ROMMON, the new image may not boot and the device stops at the rommon prompt.

Check the current ROMMON version:

show rom-monitor r0          ! ISR 4000 and similar routers
show version | include ROM   ! most platforms

Does ROMMON Need a Separate Upgrade?

  • Catalyst 9000: Usually not by hand. When a new release contains a newer ROMMON, the switch upgrades its primary ROMMON automatically at the first boot. The golden (backup) ROMMON is upgraded manually with the upgrade rom-monitor capsule golden command. The exact arguments differ by model, so check the upgrade guide for your platform.
  • ISR 4000 and similar routers: Check it every time. A well-known case is ISR 4000 routers that need ROMMON 16.12(2r) before they boot 17.x releases.

Upgrading ROMMON on an ISR 4000

ROMMON is upgraded from the running IOS-XE, not from the ROMMON prompt. Copy the ROMMON package, verify it, then:

copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/isr4200_4300_rommon_1612_2r_SPA.pkg bootflash:
verify /md5 bootflash:isr4200_4300_rommon_1612_2r_SPA.pkg
upgrade rom-monitor filename bootflash:isr4200_4300_rommon_1612_2r_SPA.pkg R0
reload
show rom-monitor r0

Do the ROMMON upgrade before the software upgrade. If you get it wrong and the device no longer boots, see Cisco ROMMON Recovery.

Secure Boot and Signed Images

IOS-XE images are signed. The .SPA in the file name stands for a signed production image. The device verifies the signature at boot. An image for the wrong platform or a corrupted file fails this check and does not boot. Only use images from Cisco Software Download and always verify the checksum.

3. Copy the Image and Verify It

FTP is faster and more reliable than TFTP for large IOS-XE images:

copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/isr4300-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin bootflash:
copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/c1100-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin bootflash:
copy tftp://192.0.2.10/cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin flash:

Setting up the server, credentials, the double slash in FTP paths and the management VRF are covered in TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades.

Verify the MD5 checksum against the value on the Cisco download page:

verify /md5 bootflash:c1100-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin

If the values differ, delete the file and copy it again. Never install an image that failed verification.

4. Upgrade in Install Mode (IOS-XE)

Install mode is the recommended mode for Catalyst 9000 switches and current ISR and Catalyst 8000 routers. One command adds, activates and commits the new software:

install add file bootflash:isr4300-universalk9.17.12.08.SPA.bin activate commit

The device asks whether it may reload. Answer y. After the reload:

show version
show install summary
install remove inactive

show install summary should show the new version as Committed. install remove inactive removes the old packages and frees space.

On Catalyst 9000 switches the command is the same, with the switch file system:

install add file flash:cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin activate commit

Several Hops in a Row

If the release notes require an intermediate release, repeat the sequence per hop: copy, verify, install add ... activate commit, check, install remove inactive. For example 17.9 first, then 17.12. Clean up between the hops so there is room for the next image.

From Bundle Mode to Install Mode

A device in bundle mode boots a .bin file directly. To switch to install mode:

  1. Run install add file <image>.bin activate commit as above. This extracts the packages and creates packages.conf.
  2. Make sure the boot variable points to packages.conf:
configure terminal
no boot system
boot system flash:packages.conf
end
write memory
show boot

On routers, use bootflash:packages.conf.

5. Bundle Mode and Classic IOS

IOS-XE in Bundle Mode, ISR G2, C900

configure terminal
no boot system
boot system bootflash:<image>.bin
end
write memory
show bootvar
reload

On classic IOS routers like the C900 series, the file system is flash: and the image name has the old format, for example c900-universalk9-mz.SPA.<version>.bin.

Classic Catalyst Switches (2960, 3560, 3750)

These switches offer archive download-sw. It transfers a .tar file, extracts it, sets the boot variable and can reload:

archive download-sw /overwrite /reload tftp://192.0.2.10/c3560-ipservicesk9-tar.<version>.tar
  • /overwrite replaces the current image when flash has room for only one.
  • /leave-old-sw keeps the old image when there is room for both. Rollback is then just a boot variable change.

Alternatively, copy the .bin file, verify it and set boot system flash:<image>.bin as above.

6. After the Upgrade

show version
show install summary          ! IOS-XE install mode
show interfaces status        ! switches
show ip interface brief
show power inline             ! PoE switches
show logging

On stacks and redundant systems, check every member: show switch on Catalyst stacks, show redundancy on dual-supervisor systems.

7. Rollback

  • Install mode: show install rollback lists the rollback points.
  • Bundle mode and classic IOS: point boot system back to the old image, if it is still in flash, and reload.
  • Device stops at ROMMON or the switch: prompt: see Cisco ROMMON Recovery.

Common Mistakes

  • Image for the wrong platform family. It fails signature or platform checks and does not boot.
  • ROMMON not checked. The new image needs a newer ROMMON, and the device stops at the rommon prompt.
  • No space for install mode. The extraction fails halfway. Run install remove inactive first.
  • Boot variable still points to the old .bin after moving to install mode. The device boots the old version in bundle mode.
  • No console access during the reload. A console server makes this possible remotely: Next-Gen Console Server Architecture.

Related Articles

  • Cisco ROMMON Recovery: Boot from Flash, TFTP or USB
  • TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades
  • Cisco Switch and Router Password Recovery
  • Cisco Nexus NX-OS Software Upgrade Guide

Sources: Cisco: Upgrading Catalyst 9500 Switches · Cisco: Upgrading Catalyst 9300 Switches

item.title: Cisco ROMMON Recovery: Boot a Switch or Router from Flash, TFTP or USB
item.description: Cisco switch or router stuck at the switch: or rommon prompt? Recovery scenarios for Catalyst 9300, 9200, 3850, 2960, 3560 and ISR 4000 — boot from flash, set ROMMON network variables, boot over TFTP or USB, and fix an outdated ROMMON.
item.content:encoded:
After a reload, the device does not come back. On the console you see only switch: (Catalyst switches) or rommon 1 > (routers). This is ROMMON, also called the boot loader: the small program that starts IOS. It stopped because it could not find or start a valid image.

This is not a hardware failure in most cases, and you do not need to replace the device. Which way out you take depends on one question: is a good image still in flash?

Scenario Situation Way out
1 The correct image is in flash Boot it, fix the boot variable
2 The image is missing or corrupted Boot over TFTP or from USB, then copy the image to flash
3 The image is there, but ROMMON is too old for it Boot an older image, upgrade ROMMON, then upgrade

Before You Start: Console Access

ROMMON is only reachable over the console. In a branch office that means a laptop and a console cable. In a data center, where you are rarely next to the rack, a console server is what makes recovery possible at all: Next-Gen Console Server Architecture.

Look at the environment first:

switch: dir flash:
switch: set

On routers:

rommon 1 > dir bootflash:
rommon 2 > set

set shows the boot loader variables. The important ones are BOOT (which image to start) and, on some switches, MANUAL_BOOT (if yes, the switch always stops at the prompt). On routers, also check the configuration register with confreg. A value of 0x2100 keeps the router in ROMMON. The normal value is 0x2102.

help or ? lists the commands your ROMMON version supports.

Scenario 1: The Correct Image Is in Flash

The image is there, but the boot variable is wrong: a typo after an upgrade, a deleted file name, or MANUAL_BOOT=yes.

Boot It Manually

Catalyst 9000 and other IOS-XE switches in install mode:

switch: boot flash:packages.conf

In bundle mode, or on classic Catalyst switches:

switch: boot flash:<image>.bin

On classic Catalyst switches, images installed with archive download-sw are in a subdirectory. Check the full path with dir flash:<directory>.

Routers:

rommon 1 > boot bootflash:<image>.bin

If the router stayed in ROMMON because of the configuration register:

rommon 1 > confreg 0x2102
rommon 2 > reset

Fix the Boot Variable in IOS

Once IOS is running, make the fix permanent, otherwise the problem returns at the next reload:

configure terminal
no boot system
boot system flash:packages.conf
end
write memory
show boot

Use the .bin file name instead of packages.conf in bundle mode, and bootflash: on routers.

Scenario 2: The Image Is Missing or Corrupted

The image was deleted by mistake, the copy was interrupted, or flash is empty. You need to bring an image to the device from outside. There are two practical ways.

TFTP from ROMMON USB
Needs someone on site No Yes
Works over a console server Yes Only if someone inserts the stick
Speed Depends on the network Fast
Typical use Data center, remote sites Branch office, lab

Option A: Boot over TFTP from ROMMON

If you are connected remotely through a console server and the network around the device works, TFTP is the most practical option. The hard part is the network configuration in ROMMON, because ROMMON has no IOS, no routing and no DHCP. You set everything by hand.

Requirements:

  • The management port is connected and reachable. On Catalyst 9000 switches that is the dedicated management port (Gi0/0). ROMMON does not use the front-panel ports.
  • A TFTP server with the image is reachable from the management network. Setup and firewall rules: TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades.

Catalyst 9000 switches:

switch: set IP_ADDRESS 192.0.2.50
switch: set IP_SUBNET_MASK 255.255.255.0
switch: set DEFAULT_GATEWAY 192.0.2.1
switch: ping 192.0.2.10
switch: boot tftp://192.0.2.10/cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin

Test with ping first. If the ping fails, there is no point starting the boot. Check the cable on the management port, the gateway and the firewall on the TFTP server.

Two limits apply, according to Cisco:

  • The switch boots in bundle mode when you boot over TFTP.
  • The image is not copied to flash. It only runs from memory. After the next reload, you are back at the prompt.

ISR 4000 and other IOS-XE routers:

rommon 1 > IP_ADDRESS=192.0.2.50
rommon 2 > IP_SUBNET_MASK=255.255.255.0
rommon 3 > DEFAULT_GATEWAY=192.0.2.1
rommon 4 > TFTP_SERVER=192.0.2.10
rommon 5 > TFTP_FILE=isr4300-universalk9.<version>.SPA.bin
rommon 6 > set
rommon 7 > boot tftp://192.0.2.10/isr4300-universalk9.<version>.SPA.bin

Variable names and the exact boot syntax differ between ROMMON versions. Check with set and help. Older routers (ISR G2) use the tftpdnld command instead, which writes the image directly to flash.

After the device has booted over TFTP: copy the image to flash, verify it and set it up properly, as described in the upgrade guide:

copy tftp://192.0.2.10/<image>.bin flash:
verify /md5 flash:<image>.bin
install add file flash:<image>.bin activate commit

On devices in bundle mode or classic IOS, set boot system to the copied file instead of install add.

Option B: Boot from USB

When someone can insert a USB stick, this is the easiest and fastest way. Format the stick with FAT32 and copy the image to it.

switch: dir usbflash0:
switch: boot usbflash0:<image>.bin

On ISR routers the USB device is usually called usb0: (on some models usb1:):

rommon 1 > dir usb0:
rommon 2 > boot usb0:<image>.bin

When the device is up, copy the image from USB to flash and fix the boot variable:

copy usbflash0:<image>.bin flash:
verify /md5 flash:<image>.bin

Then install it or set boot system as in Scenario 1.

Option C: emergency-install (Catalyst 9000)

Catalyst 9000 switches (except the 9200 series) have an emergency-install command in ROMMON. It installs an image from TFTP straight into flash:

switch: emergency-install tftp://192.0.2.10/cat9k_iosxe.<version>.SPA.bin
switch: boot flash:packages.conf

Warning: this erases the entire flash file system, including the configuration. Use it only when Options A and B are not possible, and only when you have a configuration backup.

Option D: Xmodem over the Console (Classic Catalyst)

Classic Catalyst switches like the 2960 and 3560 have no network stack in the boot loader and often no USB port. The last resort is a transfer over the console with Xmodem:

switch: flash_init
switch: set BAUD 115200
switch: copy xmodem: flash:<image>.bin

After set BAUD, change your terminal program to 115200 baud. Even at this speed the transfer takes a long time. Reset the speed afterwards with set BAUD 9600, otherwise the next person connecting at 9600 baud sees only garbage.

Scenario 3: ROMMON Is Too Old for the New Image

The image is in flash and correct, but the device still does not start it. On ISR 4000 routers this happens when the target release needs a newer ROMMON than the device has, for example 17.x releases that need ROMMON 16.12(2r).

As far as I know, ROMMON cannot be upgraded from the ROMMON prompt on these platforms. The upgrade runs from IOS-XE. The way out:

  1. Boot an older image that works with the current ROMMON. From flash if you kept it, otherwise over TFTP or USB as in Scenario 2.
  2. In IOS-XE, upgrade ROMMON: upgrade rom-monitor filename bootflash:<rommon>.pkg R0, then reload.
  3. Check with show rom-monitor r0.
  4. Now install the new image.

This is why the upgrade guide puts the ROMMON check before the upgrade.

A related case: the boot variable points to an image for another platform family, for example an ISR 4300 image on an ISR 4400. The device stays in ROMMON. Boot the correct image manually and fix the boot variable.

Prevention

  • Keep the current and the previous image on a server you can reach from the management network.
  • Check show boot (or show bootvar) and the ROMMON requirement before every planned reload.
  • Connect and test the management port before you need it.
  • Have console access ready for every upgrade: Next-Gen Console Server Architecture.

Related Articles

  • Cisco IOS and IOS-XE Upgrade Guide
  • TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades
  • Cisco Switch and Router Password Recovery
  • Cisco Nexus NX-OS Upgrade Guide (with ROMMON recovery)

Sources: Cisco: Troubleshoot Bootloader and Password Recovery on Catalyst 9000 · Cisco: ISR 4000 Stuck in ROMMON

item.title: Cisco Switch and Router Password Recovery: Catalyst 9000, 2960, 3560 and ISR
item.description: Recover a lost enable or console password on Cisco devices without losing the configuration — classic Catalyst (2960, 3560, 3750), Catalyst 9000 and 3850 with SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG, ISR routers with confreg 0x2142, and what to do when password recovery is disabled.
item.content:encoded:
You inherit a device without documentation, or a lab switch comes back from storage and asks for a password nobody knows. On Cisco switches and routers you can recover from this without losing the configuration, as long as you have physical access and a console cable.

The principle is the same everywhere: interrupt the boot, start IOS without loading the startup configuration, then put the configuration back and set new passwords. Only the way you tell the device to skip the configuration differs:

Platform Typical models How the configuration is skipped
Classic Catalyst 2960, 2960-X, 3560, 3750 Rename config.text in the boot loader
IOS-XE Catalyst 3650, 3850, 9200, 9300, 9400, 9500 SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG=1
Routers ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8000, ISR G2 Configuration register 0x2142

What You Need

  • Physical access to the device, or a console server. Password recovery is deliberately not possible over the network. See Next-Gen Console Server Architecture.
  • A console cable and a terminal program. Settings: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control.
  • A maintenance window. The device reboots and does not forward traffic during the procedure.

Switches: Get to the switch: Prompt

On Catalyst switches you interrupt the boot with the Mode button:

  1. Connect the console and open the terminal session.
  2. Unplug the power.
  3. Hold the Mode button on the front panel and reconnect the power.
  4. Keep holding until the console shows that the boot was interrupted, about 10 to 15 seconds, then release.

You are now at the switch: prompt.

On a Catalyst 9400 with two supervisors, Cisco recommends removing the secondary supervisor before you start.

Classic Catalyst (2960, 3560, 3750): Rename config.text

switch: flash_init
switch: dir flash:
switch: rename flash:config.text flash:config.text.old
switch: boot

Some older boot loaders also need load_helper after flash_init. Do not delete config.text. Renaming is enough, and you need the contents later.

The switch boots without configuration. Answer no to the initial configuration dialog, then:

Switch> enable
Switch# rename flash:config.text.old flash:config.text
Switch# copy flash:config.text system:running-config

Continue with the section “Set New Passwords and Save” below.

Catalyst 9000 and 3850: SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG

IOS-XE switches do not need the rename. A boot loader variable tells IOS to ignore the startup configuration:

switch: SWITCH_IGNORE_STARTUP_CFG=1
switch: boot flash:packages.conf

Use boot flash:<image>.bin if the switch runs in bundle mode. After the boot, answer no to the initial configuration dialog, then load the configuration:

Switch> enable
Switch# copy startup-config running-config

Important: reset the variable from IOS. Otherwise the switch ignores its configuration at every reload:

Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# no system ignore startupconfig switch all
Switch(config)# end

Continue with the next section, then save.

Routers (ISR 4000, ISR 1100, Catalyst 8000): confreg 0x2142

Routers do not have a Mode button. Interrupt the boot by sending a Break from the terminal program during the first seconds after power-on. You land at the rommon 1 > prompt.

rommon 1 > confreg 0x2142
rommon 2 > reset

The value 0x2142 tells the router to ignore the startup configuration. After the boot, answer no to the initial configuration dialog:

Router> enable
Router# copy startup-config running-config
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# config-register 0x2102

Setting the register back to 0x2102 is essential. Otherwise the router ignores its configuration at every reload.

Set New Passwords and Save

You are now in privileged mode with the original configuration loaded. Set new credentials to match how authentication was set up before:

configure terminal
enable secret <new-enable-secret>
username admin privilege 15 secret <new-password>
line con 0
 login local
line vty 0 15
 login local
end

If the device uses TACACS+ or RADIUS, check that the local fallback account works.

Copying a configuration into the running configuration merges it. Interfaces may stay administratively down, especially VLAN interfaces (SVIs) on switches. Check and fix:

show ip interface brief

Bring up interfaces that should be up with no shutdown. Then save and test:

write memory
reload

Log in with the new credentials after the reload to confirm that the configuration and the passwords survive.

When Password Recovery Is Disabled

If no service password-recovery is configured, the procedure behaves differently. The device does not let you skip the configuration. Instead it says that password recovery is disabled and asks whether to reset to the factory default configuration.

  • Yes: the configuration (and on switches the VLAN database) is deleted. The device boots with default settings. The IOS image stays.
  • No: the device boots normally with the current configuration, and you are back at the password prompt.

This is the purpose of the feature. Someone with physical access cannot read the configuration, but you lose it too. Before you answer yes, make sure you have a recent configuration backup from another source. After the reset, restore the configuration and recreate the VLANs if the backup does not contain them.

no service password-recovery makes sense for devices in public or unlocked locations, as long as the configuration is backed up somewhere else.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting config.text instead of renaming it. Only a backup helps then.
  • Forgetting no system ignore startupconfig switch all or config-register 0x2102. The device boots without configuration at the next reload.
  • Not saving after setting the passwords. The old passwords come back at the next reload.
  • SVIs left shut down after the merge. Management access over the network fails although the configuration looks correct.

Related Articles

  • Cisco ROMMON Recovery: Boot from Flash, TFTP or USB
  • Cisco IOS and IOS-XE Upgrade Guide
  • Next-Gen Console Server Architecture

Source: Cisco: Troubleshoot Bootloader and Password Recovery on Catalyst 9000

item.title: TFTP, FTP and SCP Servers for Cisco Upgrades: Setup and Troubleshooting
item.description: How to set up a TFTP, FTP or SCP server for Cisco IOS and IOS-XE image transfers on Windows, macOS and Linux — device-side commands, the management VRF, the FTP double-slash path, file size limits and firewall issues.
item.content:encoded:
Every Cisco upgrade starts with getting a file onto the device. For a 20 MB classic IOS image, almost anything works. For a 1 GB IOS-XE image over a WAN link, the choice of protocol decides whether the copy takes five minutes or fails after an hour.

This guide covers which protocol to use, how to set up the server on Windows, macOS and Linux, and the device-side commands and pitfalls.

Which Protocol?

Protocol Port Authentication Strengths Weaknesses
TFTP UDP 69 None Simple, supported everywhere, works from ROMMON Slow, unreliable over WAN, size limits on old servers
FTP TCP 21 (+ data) User and password Fast and reliable for large images Clear text, needs firewall handling for the data channel
SCP TCP 22 SSH Encrypted, uses existing SSH access Slower than FTP on some platforms
HTTP(S) TCP 80/443 Optional Fast, easy to host Not available on older IOS versions

My rule in practice:

  • FTP for normal upgrades over the network. It is fast and reliable for large IOS-XE images.
  • TFTP when the device is in ROMMON. ROMMON can only do TFTP. See Cisco ROMMON Recovery.
  • SCP when the security policy does not allow clear-text protocols.

Server Setup

Windows: Tftpd64

Tftpd64 is a free tool that combines a TFTP server, a DHCP server and a syslog server.

  1. Install Tftpd64 and start it.
  2. Set the Current Directory to the folder that contains your images.
  3. Select the Server interface, the IP address of the network adapter that faces the devices.
  4. Allow Tftpd64 in the Windows firewall. This is the most common reason why transfers time out.

For FTP on Windows, FileZilla Server is a common free choice.

macOS: Built-in TFTP Server

macOS has a TFTP server on board. It serves files from /private/tftpboot:

sudo mkdir -p /private/tftpboot
sudo cp <image>.bin /private/tftpboot/
sudo chmod 644 /private/tftpboot/<image>.bin
sudo launchctl load -F /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/tftp.plist

Stop it again with sudo launchctl unload -F /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/tftp.plist. If the macOS firewall is active, allow incoming connections.

Linux: tftpd-hpa and vsftpd

On Debian and Ubuntu:

sudo apt install tftpd-hpa

The configuration is in /etc/default/tftpd-hpa. The default directory is /srv/tftp:

TFTP_DIRECTORY="/srv/tftp"
TFTP_OPTIONS="--secure"

Add --create to TFTP_OPTIONS only if devices should be able to upload files, for example configuration backups.

For FTP, vsftpd with a local user is enough:

sudo apt install vsftpd
sudo adduser netops

Put the images in the user’s home directory or in a shared directory such as /tftpboot/images.

Device Side: Copying the Image

TFTP

copy tftp://192.0.2.10/<image>.bin flash:

FTP

Credentials can be part of the URL, or configured once:

configure terminal
ip ftp username netops
ip ftp password <password>
end
copy ftp://192.0.2.10/images/<image>.bin bootflash:

The double slash. In an FTP URL, IOS treats the path as relative to the FTP user’s home directory. If the images are in an absolute path outside the home directory, use two slashes after the server address:

copy ftp://192.0.2.10//tftpboot/images/<image>.bin bootflash:

ftp://server/images/file means <home>/images/file. ftp://server//tftpboot/images/file means /tftpboot/images/file. This detail explains many “file not found” errors.

SCP

Pulling a file from an SCP server:

copy scp://netops@192.0.2.10/images/<image>.bin flash:

Pushing a file to the device from your laptop requires the SCP server on the device:

configure terminal
ip scp server enable
end

Then from the laptop:

scp <image>.bin admin@<device-ip>:flash:<image>.bin

Disable ip scp server enable again after the transfer if your policy requires it.

Always Verify

verify /md5 flash:<image>.bin

Compare the value with the MD5 checksum on the Cisco download page. A file that copied without errors can still be incomplete.

The Management Port and VRF

On Catalyst 9000 switches, the dedicated management port (GigabitEthernet0/0) sits in its own VRF called Mgmt-vrf. On ISR 4000 and Catalyst 8000 routers, the management port is in the VRF Mgmt-intf. A copy without a VRF uses the global routing table and fails if the server is only reachable through the management network.

Tell the device which interface to use as the source:

configure terminal
ip tftp source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
ip ftp source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
end

The router management port is named GigabitEthernet0 on ISR 4000 routers. Check the name with show ip interface brief.

Troubleshooting

Timeout or “Connection refused”

  • ping the server from the device, with the right source interface or VRF.
  • Check the firewall on the server. Windows and macOS block incoming connections by default.
  • For FTP: the data channel uses additional ports. If a firewall sits between device and server, passive mode problems are common.

“File not found”

  • Check the path relative to the server’s root directory (TFTP) or the user’s home directory (FTP). Remember the double slash.
  • Check upper and lower case. File names are case-sensitive on Linux and macOS servers.
  • Check that the server user can read the file.

Copy Stops at 32 MB (TFTP)

Classic TFTP uses 512-byte blocks and a 16-bit block counter. That limits a transfer to about 32 MB unless both sides support larger blocks or block number rollover. Old or minimal TFTP servers still have this limit. IOS-XE images are much larger.

  • Use FTP or SCP for large images.
  • If you must use TFTP, use a current server and increase the block size on the device:
configure terminal
ip tftp blocksize 8192
end

Very Slow Transfer

TFTP waits for an acknowledgment after every block. Over a WAN link with high latency, that makes it extremely slow. Use FTP or SCP over long distances, or place a server close to the device.

The Legal Basis: What is Actually Mandatory?

GDPR Article 32 — Security of Processing

Source: Art. 32 GDPR

„The controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk."

This means: Every company that processes personal data — i.e., names, email addresses, health data, booking information — must set up technical protection measures. Not as a recommendation, but as a legal obligation.

BSI IT-Grundschutz — The Technical Standard

Source: BSI IT-Grundschutz Compendium

The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) defines in the IT-Grundschutz specifically what “appropriate technical measures” mean in the sense of the GDPR. German courts and data protection authorities use this standard as a guide during audits.

Does BSI IT-Grundschutz apply to small businesses? Formally, it is voluntary — but: The GDPR prescribes the “state of the art.” In Germany, this corresponds to the BSI IT-Grundschutz. Those who do not comply may have to prove during an audit why their alternative measures are equivalent.

What is Specifically Required — Measure by Measure

1. Firewall — Mandatory according to BSI NET.3.2

Legal Basis: BSI IT-Grundschutz, Building Block NET.3.2 Firewall

BSI NET.3.2.A2 stipulates:

„A rule set for the firewall must be created. No data traffic may automatically pass from the external to the internal network."

BSI NET.3.2.A9 adds:

„The firewall must log all important events."

What this means in practice:

  • A simple DSL router is not a firewall in the sense of the BSI.
  • A UTM firewall (e.g., Fortinet FortiGate, Palo Alto) is required.
  • The firewall must sit between all network zones — not just between the internet and the internal network.

Eligible for Digitalbonus: ✅ Yes — Hardware and configuration services.

2. Network Segmentation (VLANs) — Mandatory according to BSI NET.1.1 and GDPR Art. 25

Legal Basis:

  • GDPR Art. 25 — Data protection by design and by default (Privacy by Design)

„Personal data must be processed in such a way that only persons who need it for their tasks have access."

What this means in practice:

The following device classes must be operated in separate networks (VLANs):

Employee Net PCs, Laptops Access to customer data

IoT Devices Printers, IP Cameras, Smart TV, UPS Known security gaps, no updates
Guest WLAN Customers, Patients, Hotel guests Access to internal systems
POS / Checkout Card terminal, Checkout system PCI DSS obligation, payment data

Why printers are dangerous: IP printers often have outdated firmware and no automatic security updates. A compromised printer on the same network as the accounting PC gives attackers direct access to all data.

Why IP cameras are dangerous: Cheap IP cameras (Hikvision, Dahua) are regularly misused in international hacker attacks — as an entry point into the company network.

3. Guest WLAN with Captive Portal and Log Storage

Legal Basis:

  • GDPR Art. 32 — Technical protection measures

What is required:

a) Complete Isolation: The guest WLAN must have no access to internal systems. A hotel guest or patient in the waiting room must not be able to access booking systems, printers, or employee files.

b) Connection Logs — 12-month storage obligation: Anyone offering public WLAN must keep connection data (IP address, connection time, connection duration) for 12 months — for possible official inquiries.

c) Captive Portal with GDPR Consent: Upon login, the guest must be informed about data processing and actively consent.

Technical Implementation: The connection logs are captured by the firewall (e.g., FortiGate) and automatically transferred to a NAS device — stored there for 12 months.

4. Email Security — Mandatory according to BSI APP.5.3 and GDPR Art. 32

Legal Basis:

  • BSI IT-Grundschutz, Building Block APP.5.3 General Email Client and Server
  • GDPR Art. 32 — Protection against unauthorized access and data loss

BSI APP.5.3.A1 stipulates:

„Protective measures must be taken against malware in emails. Incoming and outgoing emails must be checked for malware."

What this means in practice: A simple email mailbox at Ionos or Strato without additional protection is not sufficient.

What is required:

  • Spam Filtering: Blocking of unsolicited bulk emails.
  • Malware Protection: Detection of harmful attachments (Ransomware, Trojans).
  • Phishing Protection: Detection of forged sender addresses (Business Email Compromise).
  • Logging: Proof of all filtered emails.

Technical Solution: A cloud-based Email Security Gateway (e.g., Hornetsecurity, FortiMail Cloud) routes all incoming emails through a security filter before they reach the recipient. Works with any existing email system — Office 365, Google Workspace, or simple webmail.

Eligible for Digitalbonus: ✅ Yes — as an IT security software license (up to 18 months).

5. Endpoint Protection (Antivirus / EDR) — Mandatory according to BSI SYS.2.1 and GDPR Art. 32

Legal Basis:

  • BSI IT-Grundschutz, Building Block SYS.2.1 General Client
  • GDPR Art. 32 — Protection against data loss through malware

BSI SYS.2.1.A6 stipulates:

„A virus protection program must be installed and activated on clients. The virus protection program must be updated regularly."

BSI SYS.2.1.A7 adds:

„Security-relevant events must be logged and checked for anomalies."

What this means in practice:

A single antivirus program on each PC — without central management — does not comply with the BSI standard. What is required:

  • Central Management: An administrator sees the protection status of all devices at a glance.
  • Real-time Protection: Threats are detected before they cause damage.
  • Ransomware Protection: File encryption by malware is blocked.
  • Logging: All security events are recorded — for potential audits.
  • Monthly Reports: Proof of active protective measures.

Technical Solution: Centrally managed EDR solutions like Bitdefender GravityZone or ESET Protect enable the management of all devices via a central dashboard.

Eligible for Digitalbonus: ✅ Yes — Software licenses and setup services.

6. Data Backup — Mandatory according to BSI CON.3 and GoBD

Legal Basis:

  • BSI IT-Grundschutz, Building Block CON.3 Data Backup Concept
  • GoBD (Principles of Proper Bookkeeping) — legal retention obligations
  • GDPR Art. 32 — Recoverability of personal data

BSI CON.3.A7 stipulates:

„The backed-up data must be restored regularly to check the functionality of the data backup."

The 3-2-1 Rule — Industry Standard:

  • 3 Copies of the data
  • 2 Different storage media (e.g., NAS + Cloud)
  • 1 Copy off-site (e.g., AWS Frankfurt)

What this means in practice: A single external hard drive that is occasionally manually loaded does not comply with the BSI standard. What is required:

  • Automatic daily backup — no manual intervention.
  • Encryption — data is protected even if the backup medium is stolen.
  • External copy — in case of fire or burglary, the backup remains preserved.

item.content:encoded:
You know the feeling? In the front office or at reception the Wi-Fi is perfect — but the moment you step into the meeting room, the kitchen, or the back area, the connection drops or becomes too slow for productive work.

Or at home: Netflix runs smoothly in the living room, but on the upper floor or in the garden the connection comes and goes. In a three-story villa or a luxury property on the water, strong Wi-Fi in every room seems like a dream.

It isn’t. And the best part: the problem can be solved permanently — without laying a single meter of cable.

Why Isn’t One Router Enough?

A standard router was designed for a flat of maybe 80–100 square meters. In an office with multiple rooms and thick concrete walls, or in a large house where dozens of devices connect simultaneously, a single router simply cannot cope.

The problem is not just range. Devices stubbornly cling to their current access point even when the signal is weak, instead of switching to a stronger one. This phenomenon is called the “Sticky Client” problem — and many users deal with it daily without knowing it.

The Solution: Mesh — Done Right

Mesh networks allow multiple access points to communicate with each other and form a single seamless network. But not all mesh systems are equal.

Cheap consumer mesh systems may be sufficient for a small flat. But when 30+ devices connect simultaneously in a three-story villa, or 15 employees work online in an office, these systems quickly hit their limits.

Aruba Instant On and ClientMatch Technology

Aruba is HP’s professional networking brand. The Instant On series brings enterprise know-how to small businesses and premium home users at an accessible price.

The feature that truly sets Aruba apart is ClientMatch technology:

A standard access point connects your device and then leaves it alone. You walk from room to room, but your phone stubbornly holds onto the weak access point fifteen meters behind you. ClientMatch keeps all access points in constant communication. The moment signal quality drops, the system automatically directs your device to the strongest available point — seamlessly, without interruption.

This is especially important in scenarios like:

  • Moving between floors or from the house to the garden
  • Employees moving around a large open-plan office
  • The homeowner walking between rooms during a video call

How Does It Work Without Cables?

With Aruba Instant On, access points communicate wirelessly with each other. One is connected to the internet via cable; the others are fed by it:

Internet → Modem/Router
                ↓ (cable — just this one)
         Main Aruba AP (ground floor)
                ↓ (wireless mesh)
         2nd Aruba AP (1st floor)
                ↓ (wireless mesh)
         3rd Aruba AP (2nd floor / garden)

Wherever there is a power outlet, an access point can be placed. Nothing more is needed.

The Design Works Too

Aruba Instant On devices impress not just technically but visually. Their minimalist white design fits effortlessly on a desk, a bookshelf, or next to the TV. Ceiling mounting is not required.

Beyond Wi-Fi: Switches, PoE, and Camera Integration

The Aruba Instant On ecosystem goes far beyond Wi-Fi. By adding mini PoE switches, a much more comprehensive infrastructure can be built:

What is PoE (Power over Ethernet)? Data and power are transmitted over a single Ethernet cable. For camera installations, this is a real game-changer:

Aruba PoE Switch
      ├── Aruba AP (Wi-Fi — powered via cable)
      ├── IP Camera 1 (power + data, one cable)
      ├── IP Camera 2 (power + data, one cable)
      └── IP Camera 3 (power + data, one cable)

No separate electrician needed for the cameras. A single Ethernet cable handles everything.

Security

With Aruba Instant On, the employee network and guest network are completely isolated from each other. Anyone connected to the guest Wi-Fi cannot access internal systems, NAS storage, or printers — critical for both security and GDPR compliance.

From Practice: A Law Firm

A small law firm, three office rooms. In the two back rooms where the lawyers work, the connection kept dropping. Video calls were interrupted.

The solution: two Aruba Instant On APs added — one in the corridor, one in the back office — connected via wireless mesh. Installation took two hours, during business hours, without a single minute of downtime.

The result: strong, stable connection in every corner. Separate networks for staff and clients. Video calls run smoothly.

Conclusion

Wi-Fi problems usually have a simpler solution than they first appear. No cables to lay, no walls to open up. With the right devices and ClientMatch technology, seamless, high-performance Wi-Fi is completely achievable in every corner of your office or every floor of your villa.

item.title: What Happens When the Power Goes Out? A UPS Protects Not Just Your PC — But Your Entire Office
item.description: A power outage threatens not just the computer but every device in your practice or office. Protect your NAS, switch, modem, and cameras with the right UPS.
item.content:encoded:
“UPS? Yes, we have one — it’s sitting next to the computer.”

I hear this constantly. And every time I want to ask: What about your NAS? Your switch? Your modem? Your payment terminal?

Most businesses see a UPS purely as protection against the computer shutting down unexpectedly. But during a power outage, dozens of devices in your office are at risk — and the computer is the least critical of them.

For complete data protection, pair your UPS with cloud backup: Your NAS Without RAID Is a Ticking Time Bomb

What Really Happens When the Power Goes Out?

Imagine a medical practice or a small office. When the power suddenly cuts out, all of the following go down simultaneously:

  • NAS device — a write operation is interrupted mid-process; the drive can be damaged
  • Network switch — all network connections drop
  • Modem/router — no internet
  • IP phone system — phone lines interrupted
  • Payment terminal — ongoing transaction aborted
  • Security cameras — recording stops
  • PCs — unsaved work lost

Everything goes down at once. When power returns, all devices try to boot simultaneously — this sudden load can cause further problems with weak electrical installations.

The Biggest Risk: Your NAS

Of all these devices, the NAS suffers most from a sudden power outage. A NAS is constantly writing data. If power cuts during a copy operation or scheduled backup, the write is interrupted mid-process. This can lead to filesystem corruption.

Synology and QNAP NAS devices can work directly with a UPS. Connected via USB cable, the NAS detects the moment of power loss and initiates a safe shutdown sequence:

Power cuts out
      ↓
UPS switches to battery immediately
      ↓
NAS receives signal from the UPS
      ↓
Open files are saved
      ↓
Safe shutdown in 2 minutes
      ↓
No data loss, no filesystem corruption
      ↓
Automatic restart when power returns

Without this integration, a UPS only buys you a few extra minutes — the NAS can still shut down abruptly.

UPS Types — Which One Is Right for You?

Standby (Offline) UPS The most affordable option. Sufficient for home use and simple PCs. Limited protection against voltage fluctuations.

Line-Interactive UPS The ideal choice for SMBs. Continuously regulates voltage fluctuations and switches to battery instantly on failure. Recommended type for NAS devices, switches, and critical office equipment.

Online Double Conversion UPS Highest protection class. For critical servers, medical devices, and systems that cannot tolerate any interruption.

PoE Switch: Your Cameras Are Protected Too

If you use a PoE switch (Power over Ethernet), your cameras draw power through the switch. If the switch is on the UPS, the cameras are protected too:

UPS
  ↓
PoE Switch
  ├── Camera 1 (power via switch)
  ├── Camera 2 (power via switch)
  └── NAS (connected via switch)

When power cuts, the UPS kicks in, the switch keeps running, cameras keep recording — while the NAS completes its safe shutdown.

How Many Minutes Are Enough?

For a typical office setup, 10–15 minutes is sufficient. In that time the NAS completes its safe shutdown, open documents are saved, and servers are properly shut down.

For most SMBs, 650VA–1500VA is the right range.

A Note on UPS Maintenance

UPS batteries typically need replacing every 3–5 years. With brands like APC and Eaton, the battery is modular — unscrew, swap, done. Five minutes.

I run an annual UPS check for my customers: battery capacity tested, software updates verified, NAS integration confirmed working.

Where to Start: Prioritization

  1. NAS + switch — most critical, start here
  2. Server, if present
  3. Modem/router — for internet continuity
  4. PCs — least critical

Conclusion

The right UPS, properly configured and annually maintained, brings the risk of data loss from a power outage to nearly zero. Message me on WhatsApp for a free assessment.

item.title: Does Your Website Say 'Not Secure'? Customers Leave Immediately — And SSL Certificates Are Getting Much Shorter
item.description: Expired SSL certificates cost you customers and hurt rankings. With certs shortening to 47 days, automatic SSL management is becoming essential.
item.content:encoded:
You open a website in your browser and see this in the address bar: 🔴 “Your connection is not private”

What do you do? Most likely you hit the back button.

That’s exactly what your customers do too. And you may not even notice — because an expired SSL certificate usually doesn’t notify the website owner.

What Is an SSL Certificate and Why Does It Matter?

An SSL certificate (Secure Sockets Layer) is a digital document that encrypts the connection between your website and visitors. The padlock symbol in the address bar and “https://” confirm its presence.

SSL has two core functions:

1. Security: Encrypts data flowing between the visitor’s browser and your server. A patient filling out a contact form, a customer entering payment details — this data travels encrypted.

2. Trust: When a visitor sees the padlock, they know the site is legitimate. The “not secure” warning does the opposite.

The True Cost of an Expired SSL Certificate

Many businesses treat SSL certificates as “set it and forget it.” They buy a one- or two-year certificate, it expires, they don’t notice — sometimes for weeks.

What happens during that time:

Customer loss: The vast majority of visitors who encounter a “not secure” warning leave immediately. Contact forms, appointment requests, online orders — none of it gets completed.

Google ranking drop: Google pushes sites without SSL or with expired certificates down in search results. Organic traffic built up over months can erode quickly.

Reputation damage: A customer who sees “not secure” carries a lasting negative impression of that business.

The Big Change Coming: SSL Certificates Dropping to 47 Days

Currently SSL certificates are valid for 90 days or one year. That is changing.

The CA/Browser Forum — the body that brings together certificate authorities and major browsers — has passed a new requirement: in the coming years, SSL certificate validity will drop to 47 days. Apple, Google, and Mozilla all support this decision.

What does this mean? If you currently renew once a year, you will soon need to renew 7–8 times per year. Manual tracking becomes nearly impossible.

Why was this decided? Shorter validity periods limit the impact of compromised certificates and push the industry toward automation — which is actually a positive development.

The Solution: Automatic SSL Management with Cloudflare

When Cloudflare takes over your website’s DNS, it manages your SSL certificate automatically. It renews before expiry without you needing to track anything. When validity drops to 47 days, it makes no difference — everything is handled in the background.

This feature is available even on the free Cloudflare plan.

Beyond SSL: WAF and DDoS Protection

SSL is just the beginning. When you switch to Cloudflare, you also get:

WAF (Web Application Firewall): Protects your website from SQL injection, XSS attacks, and bot traffic. Malicious requests are blocked before they reach your website.

DDoS Protection: Attack traffic aimed at taking your website down is automatically detected and filtered.

Analytics: How many visitors came, from where, how many attacks were blocked — monthly report.

No Hosting Migration Needed

The most common question: “Do I need to move my website?”

No. Cloudflare only operates at the DNS level. Your website stays where it is — Ionos, Strato, wherever. We simply move your domain’s DNS records to Cloudflare. Setup takes 1–2 hours, and your visitors notice nothing.

item.title: 🚀 Graduate Guide: What Does a Network Engineer Actually Do?
item.description: Career guide for new graduates entering network engineering. Industrial infrastructure, daily operations, and the roadmap to becoming a professional.
item.content:encoded:
Hello friends! You’ve just graduated, you have your diploma in hand, and a vast IT world lies ahead of you. While wondering “Which path should I take?”, you came across Network Engineering. So, do these people just plug in cables, or is there a massive intelligence behind the scenes? Let’s dive deep into this invisible heroism of the digital world.

🕸️ What is a Network? (A Journey on the Digital Highway)

In its simplest terms, a network is a transport vehicle that allows systems to communicate with each other. It enables computers to function not as independent islands, but as a massive, interconnected continent.

Why Isn’t a USB Drive Enough? You might use a USB drive to transfer an Excel file or a video to the computer in the next room at home. However, that’s not how things work in the professional world. Imagine you are in an office where 50 people are working on the same file, or you need to send data to a colleague in another city or even another country. In any scenario where the distance is too far or the crowd is too large for manual transfer, the Network—the digital highway—kicks in.

🏭 The Factory Example: “The Server Room” as the Heart of the System

Imagine you are in a factory. The entire memory of the factory is stored on a server in the system room: customer lists, invoices, production stocks, and employee data. Let’s assume there are 100 people in the factory. Each of these 100 people must be able to access this server from their own desk simultaneously, without errors, and at high speed.

The Network Engineer is the person who builds the road between those 100 people and that server, ensures the traffic doesn’t get congested, and secures that path. This is not just about “placing three or five boxes side by side” — it is about designing operational integrity. In today’s world, this structure is managed not only with physical cables but also with smart software layers like SD-WAN and Cloud integrations.

🏠 Home Modem vs. Industrial Infrastructure

Most of us have a modem at home, and all we do is plug it in to connect to the internet. However, in the corporate world (hospitals, hotels, plazas), these home devices are like toys:

  • Industrial Product Selection: A home-type modem will overheat, lock up, and crash when it tries to get 100 people online at once. That’s why in the professional world, we use “Industrial Switches” from global giants like Cisco, Arista, HPE (Aruba), or Juniper.
  • Ports and Connectivity: These devices usually have 24 or 48 ports. When you say an office of 100 people, don’t just count the laptops; security cameras, printers, fingerprint readers, IP phones, and Access Points are also connected to these switches. This means an office of 100 people is actually 150–200 different cable ends and connections for you to manage.

📶 Wireless World and Roaming

At home, the internet works fine near the modem but drops off in the back room. You cannot solve this with a single device in a factory or a 10-story hotel.

  • Army of Access Points (AP): Dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Access Points are installed on ceilings, in warehouses, and in offices.
  • Seamless Transition (Roaming): Imagine walking from one end of a factory to the other while on a call with your laptop. The internet must not drop for even a second. Your expertise lies in setting up and managing that smart structure (Wireless Controller) that allows your device to drop one AP and latch onto another without you even noticing.

🛡️ The Gatekeeper of the Internet: Firewall and Leased Lines

Corporate internet operates under much different rules than home internet:

  • Metro Ethernet (Dedicated): At home, the internet slows down in the evening because you share the line with your neighbors. In companies, “Dedicated” (exclusive to you) lines are used. Your speed is always constant, and most importantly, your Upload speed is very high.
  • Firewall: We place a sentry at the entrance of this valuable internet line. With brands like Palo Alto, Fortinet, or Check Point, you implement who can access which site, how external cyberattacks are blocked, and the Zero Trust philosophy.

Want to understand Zero Trust from an architecture perspective? The Zero Trust Mindset: Engineering Security as an Architecture, Not a Product

🌙 The Other Side of the Coin: Shifts and Responsibility

If you are going to be a network engineer, you must accept this reality: “The system is never shut down while everyone is working.”

  • Maintenance Windows: If you are going to update the software inside a switch or change the location of cables, you can’t do this while everyone is in the office. This is why work is often done during late-night hours, weekends, or public holidays.
  • Sleepless Nights and Rights: Your phone might ring at 3:00 AM if the system crashes. However, in the professional world, this is a sacrifice, and companies usually balance this by offering overtime pay or “service time” (extra time off) during the week.

🎓 Roadmap: How to Become a Network Engineer?

This profession is learned not just by reading, but by doing and following globally recognized paths:

  1. The Foundation of Certification: CCNA This is the “driver’s license” of the network world. Cisco Certified Network Associate (CCNA) training allows you to learn the alphabet of the business (IP, Routing, Switching).

  2. Official Education Portals (The Treasure Trove!) Manufacturers offer great resources for you to learn their devices:

    • Cisco Networking Academy (Skills for All): skillsforall.com
    • Palo Alto Networks Education: learning.paloaltonetworks.com
    • Fortinet Training Institute: training.fortinet.com
    • Aruba (HPE) Learning Center: learn.hpe.com/aruba
    • Juniper Learning Portal: learningportal.juniper.net

  3. Online and Self-Learning

    • Udemy: You can find very affordable CCNA courses in many languages.
    • CBT Nuggets: The video explanations are of very high quality.
    • Simulation Tools: Don’t just read books! Install Cisco Packet Tracer on your computer. For more advanced levels, use GNS3 or EVE-NG to experience professional device software.

Conclusion

Networking is the foundation of computing. Whether you are a developer or a cybersecurity specialist, you cannot be a true professional without knowing how a packet gets from point A to point B. If you love solving complex puzzles and building the infrastructure of digital worlds, Network Engineering is a prestigious and exciting career path that is always in demand.

item.title: Your NAS Without RAID Is a Ticking Time Bomb — And the Fix Costs €1 a Month
item.description: NAS without RAID is a serious business risk. How AWS S3 automatic encrypted backup works and why Glacier costs as little as €1 per month.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine a medical practice. Eight years of patient records, invoices, reports. All on a small NAS device in the office. One morning the device doesn’t start. Hard drive failure. You call a data recovery company — “we’ll try, €800–2000, no guarantee.”

This scenario happens every day. And preventing it costs just a few euros a month.

The Misconception: “I Have a NAS, So I Have a Backup”

A NAS (Network Attached Storage) is an excellent device — central storage, accessible from every computer on the network. But most NAS devices in small businesses run with a single hard drive. No RAID.

What is RAID? RAID writes data to multiple drives simultaneously. In its simplest form, RAID 1 writes the same data to two drives at once. If one fails, the other takes over. No data loss.

With a NAS running a single drive without RAID, the moment that drive fails, everything is gone. No warning, no recovery.

“But my NAS has RAID” — good, but not enough. RAID protects against drive failure. It does not protect against fire, water damage, theft, ransomware, or accidental deletion. An external backup is essential.

The Solution: AWS S3 Cloud Backup

AWS S3 (Simple Storage Service) is Amazon’s cloud storage service. It sounds like something for large corporations — but small businesses can use it for just a few euros a month.

How it works:

NAS device (Synology/QNAP)
        ↓ (automatic, nightly)
Hyper Backup software
        ↓ (encrypted)
AWS S3 — Frankfurt (eu-central-1)
        ↓
Your data: secure, encrypted, redundant

Synology NAS devices have a built-in “Hyper Backup” application. You configure it once, and every night it automatically sends changed files to S3. Your backup runs while you sleep.

AWS S3 Storage Tiers — Which One Is Right for You?

Tier Best for Access Cost
S3 Standard Frequently accessed data Instant ~€23/TB/month
S3 Infrequent Access A few times per month Instant ~€12/TB/month
S3 Glacier Instant Rarely accessed archives Milliseconds ~€4/TB/month
S3 Glacier Deep Archive Long-term archiving 12 hours ~€1/TB/month

Recommendation for SMBs: Active business data: S3 Infrequent Access — affordable, instant access when needed. Older records and archive files: S3 Glacier Instant — very low cost, still instantly retrievable.

A typical scenario for a medical practice: active patient data in S3 IA (€5–8/month), older archive years in Glacier (€1–2/month). Total monthly cost: €6–10.

GDPR and Legal Aspects

If you process patient, client, or customer data, you are subject to GDPR. Two things are critical for cloud backups:

1. Frankfurt region (eu-central-1) is mandatory — your data must remain within EU borders.

2. Encryption is mandatory — Hyper Backup encrypts your data before sending it to S3. The encryption key stays with you — not even AWS can view the contents.

3. The account is in your name — I open a separate AWS account for each customer in your name. The data and the account belong entirely to you.

For medical practices and law firms I also prepare a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) — required under GDPR.

How Does the Setup Work?

  1. AWS account opened in your name
  2. S3 bucket created with correct tier and lifecycle policies
  3. Hyper Backup installed on your NAS
  4. First full backup created
  5. From the next day, only changed files are sent
  6. Monthly status report by email

What you need to do after setup: Nothing. Everything runs automatically.

What If I Don’t Have a NAS?

S3 backup is also possible without a NAS. We install a small backup agent on your PCs (Duplicati — free), and selected folders are automatically sent to S3.

Conclusion

A NAS with a single drive can fail at any time without warning. Even a RAID NAS does not protect against ransomware or physical damage. With AWS S3, your data is encrypted, redundant, and safe for just a few euros a month.

The account is yours, the data is yours, the encryption key is yours.

item.title: 🛠️ The Backdoor of the Network: Next-Gen Console Server (Terminal Server) Architecture
item.description: Survival guide for lost IP access to critical infrastructure. Out-of-Band Management, HTML5 CLI, and automation-ready console servers explained.
item.content:encoded:
A network engineer’s biggest nightmare is the complete loss of IP access to a critical device at a remote location. A wrong switchport command, a faulty ACL, or a device freeze… In these cases, when you cannot reach the management IP, you are forced to travel for hours for “on-site intervention” or send someone else. This is exactly where the Console Server (Terminal Server), the “insurance” of the network, comes into play.

However, today these devices have evolved into security and automation-oriented professional management platforms that offer much more than a simple serial port multiplexer.

This article is part of a broader series on resilient network design. For the architectural foundation: IT Infrastructure Is Not a Collection of Products

1. Why Do We Need a 48-Port Management Giant?

In enterprise-level data centers, dozens of switches, routers, firewalls, and servers are located in the same cabinet. A 48-port console device allows you to manage an entire cabinet via a single IP, optimizing physical space and ending cabling chaos.

  • Space Saving: Taking console control of 48 devices in a single U (unit) space simplifies the intra-cabinet architecture.
  • Centralized Entry: By providing access to all devices through a single portal, you minimize management complexity.

2. Smart Ports: Software-Selectable Pinout for Every Device

Every manufacturer (Cisco, Juniper, HP, Palo Alto, etc.) has different console standards and pinouts. We used to have to carry different adapters (dongles) or custom-made cables for every brand. The greatest strength of modern console servers is the Software-Selectable Pinout feature:

  • Software Flexibility: Different Baud Rate, Data Bits, and most importantly, Pinout settings can be defined independently for each port.
  • Adapter-free Connection: Thanks to software pinout, you can connect to any brand with a standard CAT6 cable without the need for complex converter adapters. This is the ultimate solution to “cable soup” chaos.

3. Flexible Access: HTML5 Web CLI and Software Integration

Diversity in access methods provides engineers with tremendous agility during a crisis:

  • Java-Independent HTML5 Support: Say goodbye to the clunky Java applications that were the biggest problem with old-gen devices. You can now open secure and high-speed CLI sessions directly through modern web browsers without installing any applications.
  • SecureCRT and SuperPutty Integration: Fully compatible with your favorite CLI software. You can connect to devices over SSH tunnels with a single click through terminal emulators you are used to, managing your sessions professionally. This integration is vital for bulk-pasting complex command sets.

4. Security and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC & TACACS+)

The console port is the “backdoor” of a device, and this door must be protected at the highest level. Someone connecting to a device via console that cannot be reached over IP is touching the very heart of the device.

  • Centralized Authorization: Centralized management is provided through TACACS+, RADIUS, or LDAP integration. You can track who entered which port, at what time, and for how long, second by second.
  • Role-Based Access (RBAC): Define permissions only for the ports each user is responsible for. For example, let the security team see only Firewall consoles, while the systems team accesses only server consoles.
  • Advanced API Support: Bulk commands can be sent to devices via API, or configurations can be automated based on instantaneous conditions.

5. Automation and Traceability: CLI Logging & Config Backup

A console server is no longer just a bridge; it is a recording and post-mortem analysis center:

  • Automatic CLI Output Logging: All CLI outputs flowing on the console screen are automatically recorded. When a device crashes or gives a Kernel Panic, you cannot see the logs at that moment because the device has no IP access. However, since the console server records this stream, you can analyze the device’s last “cries” before the crash and find the root cause in seconds.
  • Automatic Configuration Backup: Both the console device’s own settings and the critical configurations of the devices it manages are periodically backed up. This is part of the Network Infrastructure as Code (NIAC) vision.

6. Uninterrupted Access: Dual WAN and Out-of-Band (OOBM) Architecture

If the network has completely collapsed, how will you reach the console server? This is where real “engineering” begins:

  • Dual WAN & Cellular Support: With two independent internet inputs or internal 4G/5G LTE modules, you continue to reach devices over the cellular network even if your main internet line is cut.
  • Out-of-Band Management (OOBM): This isolated path, established over a different service provider completely independent of main data traffic, is the only lifebuoy that gives you a chance to intervene even when the main network is completely “down.”

7. Market Leaders

The following brands set the market standards in high port density, smart automation features, and HTML5 support:

  • Opengear: At the top with smart OOBM and high-security features.
  • Lantronix: Known for flexible port structures and ease of management.
  • Avocent (Vertiv) & Perle: Indispensable for professional data centers with their stable hardware.

Conclusion

The console server is the invisible protector of a complex infrastructure. These features, ranging from SecureCRT integration to automatic CLI logging, and from adapter-free connection to Java-independent HTML5 support, turn crisis moments into manageable operations.

Remember: the best network is the one that always has a “Plan B.”

item.title: 🛡️ Visibility and Security Strategy in Enterprise Networks: Network Packet Broker (NPB) Masterclass
item.description: Strategic guide for traffic management, cybersecurity, and end-to-end visibility in enterprise networks. What is NPB? How to manage it with NIAC principles?
item.content:encoded:
In today’s enterprise network architectures, “speed” is no longer the sole criterion for success. The real challenge is knowing what flows within tens of gigabits of data traffic per second, ensuring security, and monitoring performance end-to-end. As the “intelligent traffic conductor” of modern networks, the Network Packet Broker (NPB) has become a strategic necessity for everything from cybersecurity to business continuity.

For the broader architecture context behind visibility strategy, see: IT Infrastructure Is Not a Collection of Products

1. Micro-Second Precision: End of Packet Loss (Buffering & Time-Stamping)

Network traffic does not always flow linearly; instantaneous bursts occur. While many standard switches drop packets during these bursts, a professional NPB solves this problem at the hardware level:

  • 500 ms Buffer Memory: NPB holds traffic momentarily in its memory, reducing packet loss to 0% during times when your analysis tools (DLP, IDS, Sniffer) cannot keep up with the speed. This is vital for forensics and debugging processes.
  • Hardware Time-Stamping: When performing latency analysis, “about an hour” is not a professional answer. With the hardware Time-Stamping feature offered by NPBs, you can stamp every packet with micro-second precision the moment it enters the system. These stamps are life-savers, especially in forensic analysis processes.

2. Intelligent Filtering and Protocol Mastery (L2-L4)

While L2-4 filtering (MAC, IP, Port) exists in many devices, the difference with an NPB is that it performs this process at “wire-speed” without compromising packet integrity and with unparalleled flexibility:

  • Flow Aggregation & Deduplication: It analyzes thousands of flows coming from massive 100 GB inputs, cleans duplicate packets (Deduplication), and converts all this chaos into a single optimized flow for analysis devices. Cleaning duplicate packets reduces the CPU load of your analysis devices by 30-50%.
  • Packet Slicing (Lighten the Load): You don’t always need to be in love with the entire packet. If your analysis tool only needs header information, perform Packet Slicing on the NPB to trim the payload. This way, you don’t overwhelm the disks and processors of your analysis devices with unnecessary data, gaining 100% efficiency.

3. Flexible Delivery Methods: Getting Traffic to the Target

NPB offers a rich “packaging” menu to deliver your filtered traffic to the analysis device:

  • ERSPAN & VXLAN/GRE Tunneling: It carries traffic to remote data centers or cloud-based analysis centers by encapsulating it over Layer 3 networks.
  • VLAN Tagging / Stripping: It adds tags for the analysis device to recognize the traffic or cleans these tags to lighten the load on the device.
  • Load Balancing: It distributes dense 100G traffic equally to 10G capacity analysis devices without breaking “session stickiness” (session integrity).

4. API Support, Automation, and the NIAC Vision

Manual intervention is a risk in modern IT operations. The automation capabilities offered by NPB provide agility to teams. However, do not view the process as just a simple “backup”; we integrate these devices into Network Infrastructure as Code (NIAC) principles thanks to Rest-API support.

  • NIAC & Disaster Recovery (DR): All critical filtering rules and port configurations on the device should be managed with NIAC principles. In the event of a hardware failure, we can migrate the entire architecture to a new device in seconds using automation scripts rather than manual configuration.
  • ITSM and SIEM Integration: During a cyber incident, filters can be automatically created via SIEM tools, or existing filters can be edited via API according to the instantaneous situation.

5. Performance and Security (Riverbed, DLP & SSL Offloading)

NPB is like a central “Data Hub” feeding all kinds of analysis devices on the network:

  • Network TAP (Inline Data Collection): It can receive traffic directly from cables going to servers (Network TAP), not just switch ports. This allows you to reach the “purest” data without affecting main traffic.
  • SSL/TLS Offloading: Don’t exhaust the CPUs of your Firewall or IPS devices with decryption. Handle this load on the NPB and send “clean” and unencrypted traffic to analysis devices. Let your security devices do their actual job; let the NPB handle the heavy lifting of decryption.
  • Riverbed Integration: By feeding NPM devices like Riverbed with the most accurate data, it detects application latencies and bottlenecks.
  • Call Centers (VoIP): It processes voice traffic in parallel; while one copy goes to the recording system, the user continues the conversation without any delay.

6. Encrypted Traffic and Data Center (DC) Strategy

Although internet traffic is encrypted, “East-West” traffic flowing unencrypted within the data center for performance reasons is still the biggest opportunity. Using NPB at these strategic points where traffic is transparent and mirroring the data provides 100% visibility without incurring decryption costs.

7. Market Leaders

While Keysight (Ixia) and Gigamon set the standards for high-performance solutions; brands like Arista, Garland Technology, and Profitap are indispensable for enterprise networks with their flexible port structures and innovative delivery methods.

Conclusion

The seamless orchestration of traffic mirroring and analysis flows is the definitive proof of how a complex network operation can be rendered controllable. By leveraging NIAC (Network Infrastructure as Code) and robust API integrations, this architecture transforms from a static hardware setup into a dynamic, “living” security platform.

Such a framework ensures that critical data reaches security tools with zero loss and maximum optimization, granting operational teams full visibility and command over the network.

item.title: The Product-Centric Trap in IT: Standards vs. Brands
item.description: Why engineering mindset and documentation outweigh product knowledge in IT. Analysis of common misconceptions in IT recruitment and management.
item.content:encoded:
In the modern IT landscape, job descriptions often read like a “superhero” wish list. Candidates are expected to have deep expertise in dozens of competing products — Fortinet, Cisco, Palo Alto, Check Point — simultaneously. However, there is a fundamental logic gap here: why would a professional who is a master of all these domains want to work in an environment that lacks clear standards and processes?

For the architectural thinking behind this topic, see: IT Infrastructure Is Not a Collection of Products

1. The “Superhero” Recruitment Paradox

Many companies create job postings with excessive expectations, listing every technology they can think of. Yet, the candidates they find rarely meet the actual needs of the business.

The real issue is often not a lack of technical skill, but a lack of internal processes. Instead of looking for a person who knows every brand, companies should focus on defining how their own systems work.

2. Product Knowledge vs. Engineering Vision

Security and network policies should be a corporate culture, independent of brands. For a competent engineer, different interfaces are just tools. A professional who masters core network and security logic (TCP/IP, routing, policy management) can adapt from Palo Alto to Fortinet in a very short time.

The critical question for a company is not “Which brand do you know?” but rather:

  • “How do we access the internet?”
  • “What is our standard for writing a firewall rule?”

If these answers are documented, the system administrator spends their energy on efficiency rather than reinventing the wheel every time someone new joins the team.

For a deeper look at how product selection relates to architecture: Network Infrastructure Product Selection: Strategic Criteria

3. The Power of Planning and Documentation

In IT projects, planning is often dismissed as a “waste of time.” However, a well-planned system and detailed documentation are the foundation of institutional memory.

This documentation process cannot be a burden placed solely on the shoulders of a new hire; it is a management style that senior leaders must establish together.

For a practical example of how documentation aids operational success, see: Cisco Nexus NX-OS Software Upgrade Guide

4. Visibility and Request Management (ITSM)

A common complaint among IT teams is that their work is “invisible.” In organizations where ITSM (IT Service Management) tools are not used and requests are not recorded:

  • The time spent on tasks cannot be reported.
  • Changes made on the system cannot be audited.
  • The actual performance of the IT team becomes unmeasurable.

Without visibility, IT operates in survival mode — reacting to fires rather than preventing them. ITSM tooling is not a bureaucratic overhead; it is the mechanism that makes IT work legible to the rest of the organization.

On making IT operations proactively visible: Monitoring Done Right: How to Build a Proactive IT Operations Culture

5. Management’s Responsibility: Budget, Time, and Resources

The most critical role belongs to senior management. Without a mandate from the top, standardization remains a dream. If managers do not provide:

  1. Sufficient Budget
  2. Reasonable Time
  3. Correct Human Resources

Teams will be forced to work in “emergency mode,” focusing only on surviving the day rather than following standards. The best engineers cannot build institutional quality without organizational support.

Conclusion

Companies should not expect miracles simply by hiring “star players” without first establishing a solid backbone of processes. Corporate success is a product of a well-designed system — not just talented individuals.
